results.title: Can a Photo Timestamp Be Faked? | Timemark
results.content:
### How to verify a Timemark photo

Anyone can check a supported photo for free without installing the app:

1. Go to verify.timemark.com, or select Verify Photos at the top of the Timemark app.
2. Upload the photo containing its visible Photo Code.
3. Review the checks for Time & Date, Location and Image Analysis.
4. Read the result: Authentic, Fake, Unable to Verify or Not Found.

Image Analysis compares the uploaded picture with features recorded at capture. It is designed to tolerate normal compression, which is common when photos are shared.

## What photo verification cannot prove

Time and location verification does not prove that the scene itself is genuine. Someone could stage a scene, photograph another screen or place an object in view. [...] On both iPhone and Android, Timemark also detects a mock GPS location. When that happens, the address printed on the photo says Virtual location detected.

A Timemark photo with a valid Photo Code has that code printed on the image. The code connects to the original time, location and picture features recorded at capture and kept on Timemark's servers. Editing the image file or its EXIF does not change that separate record.

If Timemark detects a modified app, or cannot confirm the device is safe after a long period offline, the photo receives no valid Photo Code. Normal offline photos can still show the real time and carry a Photo Code. They can be verified after the phone reconnects.

You can read more about how Timemark photo verification works.

results.title: How to prove a picture was taken before a certain date?
results.content:
Add a comment|

 blockchain for that.

Create a file with both your original file (in case of text it can be inline, otherwise use a container like a ZIP archive) as well as a message stating who you are and that you have a copy of the file. Take the SHA1 of the resulting file/container and use it as a Bitcoin address to send some coins to. This will permanently store the hash in the blockchain with a timestamp precise up to a few hours.

This is anonymous and doesn't reveal anything about the file, but when the time comes you can just reveal the hashed file as well as the hash and anyone can verify the timestamp independently.

There are easy to use services for that which you may want to check out, though I haven't used them personally and I can't vouch for them.

Share [...] So, for your situation: it sounds like somebody is requiring you to do this (maybe for legal reasons?). You should find out level of trust they need in the timstamping authority. What you have come up with is to use Picassa or Flickr as a trusted Timestamping Authority. Depending on what you need the timestamp for, that might be ok. For example, if it's your friend to win a bet, then the `upload time` on Picassa or Flickr is probably fine. If this is to prove ownership of multi-billion dollar real estate holdings, then you may want to involve a notary. [...] 6  Note that you can't use the result of a hash function as a bitcoin address directly, as they contain error detection information. You'll need to craft the transaction manually.
